Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-12

Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Theo (Redwood SE), Lena (Orchid ML), Marco (Orchid Infra), Priya (CTO), Aaron (SRE)

Auto-summary (auto gen, may be rough):
Quick deep dive on GPU serving hysteresis behaviour when using continuous batching + K-V cache; shown TRT-LLM fallback traces vs vllm path, discussed cudagraph replay instability when eviction/prefetch interacts with persistent KV. Agreed on pilot to run traces with representative prompts + NVLink pinned config.

Topics: GPU kernel path selection, eviction-induced latency spikes, cudagraph replay vs dynamic kernel path, quantization tradeoffs, VPC/on-prem constraints for private deployment.

--- Transcript body ---
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out the hour. We're going to zoom in on the tail-latency behavior you saw in the pilot cluster, uh, dig into kernel timelines and see why those spikes show up. Theo and I will walk through the traces.
[00:20] Lena: Thanks. We had a couple of very nasty 99.9 spikes last week. It was like nothing in the app changed, but latency doubled for a burst. We captured perf counters but looking for your read.
[00:34] Theo: Yep, we saw that. Important context: you're running a mixed-size workload — short chatty prompts plus some 2k-token summarizations — and you had prefix caching enabled plus a persistent KV path, right?
[00:47] Marco: Correct, we keep K-V caching on, persistent mode. We're also on a set of A100s with NVLink in the private rack, and it's behind a VPC with strict egress rules.
[01:02] Theo: Got it. So two axes to look at: kernel selection and cudagraph replay. When the runtime decides between the fast fused-kernel path and a slower fallback, that decision can flip if the sequence length distribution changes mid-batch. That flip is what we sometimes call hysteresis.
[01:23] Priya: Hysteresis as in the runtime oscillates between exec paths? I thought that was only theoretical.
[01:28] Theo: In practice it happens when batches include both cached prefixes and new contexts; the KV cache can change the expected shape, and cudagraphs that were compiled for one shape may be replayed for another, causing re-submissions or even fallback to a non-graph path.
[01:44] Aaron: And we saw cudagraph errors in GPU logs around the same timestamps — CUDA graph replay failed, then kernel fallback, then a big latency hit.
[01:52] Maya: I'll share the trace we annotated. (link: drive.google.com/benchmarks/orchid-aug-traces)
[02:00] Lena: Thanks. Looking at these, I also see memory pressure before the spike. Could eviction be triggering cudagraph instability?
[02:10] Theo: Yes — if the runtime evicts KV cache pages during a graph replay, the next inference sees a different KV layout. CudaGraph replay assumes deterministic kernels and buffer placements; when those differ, either you get an assert or the runtime falls back mid-execution.
[02:27] Lena: So eviction correlates with the 99.9 spikes. Any mitigation patterns?
[02:32] Theo: A few. One: prefer a persistent-KV allocation that pins buffers so eviction is less likely. Two: use smaller graph segments or avoid full-sequence graphs for highly variable sequence lengths — that reduces fragility. Three: add a hysteresis policy in routing so we don't mix very short and very long requests in the same batch.
[02:49] Marco: For us pinning isn't ideal because memory is tight. Can we get similar behavior with quantization to reduce footprint?
[02:56] Theo: Quant helps. INT8/4-bit reduces memory and kernel runtime, but quantized kernels sometimes use different fused ops which change kernel selection. There's a balancing act: quant reduces overall footprint so eviction is less frequent, but you might see different kernel paths and slightly different latency characteristics.
[03:14] Priya: How did TenserRT LLM compare? I remember earlier you said TRT-LLM had a more deterministic graph path.
[03:21] Theo: TRT-LLM tends to compile larger fused kernels and is more aggressive with graph capture. That gives great throughput, but it's less forgiving when input shapes vary or when persistent KV layout changes. vllm's path is more dynamic — it can be slower in steady state but recovers from layout changes more gracefully.
[03:40] Maya: Worth mentioning we have hybrid profiles — Redwood can route latency-sensitive short queries to a low-latency instance class and heavy long jobs to a throughput-optimized cluster. That routing reduces the risk of mixed-shape batching.
[03:54] Aaron: We liked the idea of routing, but our user traffic shifts rapidly during morning syncs. Can we set an autoscaling and routing hysteresis window?
[04:03] Theo: Absolutely. You can configure time-based routing thresholds and a minimum hold period so once a path is selected it won't flip for X seconds. That buys you stability for cudagraph-backed kernels.
[04:15] Lena: There's also the prefetch/prefill behavior — we warm prefixes for common prompts which reduces token compute but increases memory usage. Is there a technique to reduce eviction risk while keeping warmed prefixes?
[04:26] Theo: We often use an LRU with weighted eviction that biases retention towards high-hit prefixes. Also, prefix compression or dedup can reduce KV size. Another newer pattern is sharding the KV cache per worker to avoid global evictions that change memory layouts.
[04:43] Marco: Per-worker sharding sounds interesting. Does it hurt cache hit rate?
[04:47] Theo: Slightly — hit rate drops a bit, but the tradeoff is stability: isolated workers have stable buffer addresses so cudagraph replay is reliable. We can show you hit/miss tradeoffs in the pilot.
[04:58] Priya: Can you show us a kernel timeline?
[05:01] Theo: Sure — I'm pulling up a trace. (pause) Right here: you can see at t+0.6s we capture a big fused attention kernel, then at t+1.1s eviction happens and at t+1.12s the runtime falls back to a non-fused path — that's the 600ms spike. The GPU SM utilization drops briefly while the fallback kernels recompile or select different kernels.
[05:28] Lena: That aligns with our logs. There's a question about cudagraph replay errors though — are these deterministic or intermittent?
[05:35] Theo: We saw both. Often intermittent and triggered by particular mixing patterns. In one case, a background job writing to the KMS triggered a timing change that coincided with eviction and the graph failed. Small differences cascade.
[05:47] Maya: Actionable mitigation checklist so far: pin critical KV regions, shard per worker, add routing hysteresis, consider quantization carefully, and smaller graph capture windows.
[05:58] Aaron: On the network side: our VPC adds 1-2ms of headroom occasionally. Does Redwood's private deploy require any special MTU or NIC settings for NVLink?
[06:08] Theo: NVLink is on the PCI fabric — network settings don't affect NVLink itself, but RDMA or EFA settings do matter for multi-host aggregation. For single-host NVLink pools, ensure the driver and MIG settings are consistent. We have a private-deploy checklist that lists kernel/driver versions; I'll attach that.
[06:26] Maya: (link: go.redwood.docs/private-deploy-checklist)
[06:30] Priya: Good. Another dimension: model quantization + calibration. How safe is 4-bit for our legal summarization workloads? We need near-identical ROUGE/QA performance.
[06:41] Theo: For legal text, we recommend mixed calibrations — keep the LM head in higher precision and quantize attention / FFN where possible. Also run evals on your prompt set. Redwood Optimize can suggest quant profiles tuned to your prompts and show the quality delta.
[06:56] Lena: Would that change kernel selection significantly?
[06:59] Theo: Yes. INT8/4-bit kernels invoke different fused ops; sometimes TRT-compiled kernels are preferred for quant paths because they include quant-friendly fused ops. That means the hysteresis window might change after quantization, so plan a staged rollout.
[07:14] Marco: In our environment we have strict KMS policies — can Redwood integrate with our HSM for KMS?
[07:21] Maya: Yes, private deployments support customer-managed KMS/HSM and we can document key rotation and audit exports. We'll include the security questionnaire.
[07:31] Priya: Great. Back to the kernel convo — you mentioned cudagraph capture windows. If we reduce capture length, do we lose throughput?
[07:39] Theo: Some throughput is sacrificed because shorter graphs mean more host-driver interactions. But the reliability gains often outweigh the throughput loss for variable workloads. You can do adaptive capture: capture for the common short shape and fall back to driver paths for longer sequences.
[07:53] Lena: Is there a cost or latency difference between vllm fallback vs TRT's fallback?
[07:58] Theo: vllm's fallback is usually less of a cliff — it degrades gradually. TRT fallback can be sharp because you're switching from large fused kernels to element-wise kernels. That's why we suggested routing short queries to low-latency instances and long ones to throughput nodes.
[08:12] Aaron: We plan to keep a warm pool for interactive queries. How quickly can Redwood scale that?
[08:17] Maya: With Dedicated you can reserve warm nodes and have burst capacity. Autoscaling down has a cooling period; we can set policies to keep N nodes warm during business hours.
[08:27] Priya: Regarding logs and observability, can we get token-level latency traces to link spikes back to kernel events?
[08:34] Theo: Yes — we export per-request token timelines including kernel names, CUDA events, and SM utilization. We'll send the raw trace format so you can overlay it with your perf counters.
[08:45] Maya: Attaching initial sample: (link: drive.google.com/orchid-gpu-trace-sample)
[08:50] Lena: Good. On benchmarking: we want to run a pilot that compares three configs: 1) TRT-LLM heavy graph capture, 2) vllm dynamic path with persistent KV pinned, 3) hybrid routing. Proposed window: 48-72 hours each.
[09:05] Theo: Sounds reasonable. For the TRT config, we'll lock driver/kernel versions and compile the graphs upfront. For vllm config, we'll disable large graph capture and enable per-worker shard KV. Hybrid is the routing rules.
[09:18] Marco: Any test harness recommendations? We use Locust for load but need a token-level generator.
[09:24] Theo: We can share our bench harness (redwood-bench) — it includes a synthetic prompt generator that preserves token length distributions and simulates burstiness. We'll give you a small runner to integrate with Locust.
[09:36] Maya: (link: github.com/redwood/bench-orchid-runner)
[09:40] Priya: Ok, timeline: if you run TRT vs vllm for 72 hours each, when can we get results?
[09:46] Theo: If we start Aug 24, we can have initial artifacts and a debrief the week of Aug 31. We'll include latency percentiles, eviction counts, cudagraph failures, and kernel timelines.
[09:57] Maya: I'll capture that in next steps.
[10:01] Lena: Small question: do we need to reboot nodes when switching quant profiles?
[10:05] Theo: Some runtimes allow on-the-fly swapping with rolling restarts of worker processes, but for large quant changes a full driver restart can be safer. We'll note a minimal-downtime process in the playbook.
[10:17] Aaron: Any competitor pitfalls we should avoid? We tested ManagedEndpointX and they had a cold-graph problem where their capture strategy caused 10s of seconds of recompile on first mixed batch.
[10:28] Theo: Yeah, we've seen that pattern in market tools. That's why staged capture and hysteresis matter.
[10:34] Priya: Any final security notes re private deploy?
[10:38] Maya: We'll provide the SOC2/ISO summary, and our private deploy supports customer VPC, SAML SSO, and KMS integration. Expect a standard compliance packet.
[10:49] Lena: Great.
[10:51] Theo: Quick note about observability — when you run the pilot, please enable token-level tracing and set high-resolution sampling for the 99.9 window. That gives us the signal we need to diagnose microspikes.
[11:03] Maya: Ok let's recap actions.
[11:05] Maya: Theo will attach cudagraph replay traces and kernel timelines. Lena will send the prompt set and the real percentile targets. Marco will confirm NVLink / network constraints and KMS vendor. Maya will send private-deploy pricing and security questionnaire. We'll schedule the pilot for Aug 24 start and check in Aug 31.
